narrative: During the 2010s, Black and African women's hairstyles continued to thrive as a vital part of their cultural identity. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s but resurged in popularity in the 2000s, encouraged people of sub-Saharan African descent to celebrate their afro-textured hair. Styles like the afro, cornrows, and box braids became increasingly popular as protective hairstyles that not only reduced breakage but also showcased the beauty and versatility of Afro-textured hair. Dreadlocks, Bantu knots, and locs were also worn with pride, demonstrating a deep connection to African culture and heritage. These hairstyles were not just about aesthetics; they represented resistance against Eurocentric beauty standards and a celebration of Black identity. While the source material does not provide extensive documentation on this decade specifically, it is clear that the 2010s saw a continued growth in self-expression and empowerment through hair culture among Black and African women.
